en: Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Mañjuśrī, the Youthful!

The earth shines with the rows of parasols and sunshades held aloft in the expanse of the sky—white as a conch shell, milk, the moon, jasmine, crystal, snow, fine linen, and a pure white cloud; resplendent with loud, clear laughter; and honored by the gods, humans, garuḍas, siddhas, and gandharvas.
All of them, bowing low, constantly pay homage to that Buddha, the kinsman of the sun,
with heaps of divine sandalwood powder wafted by gentle breezes,
and with the sounds of lutes, flutes, mṛdaṅga drums, and dundubhi drums, and with the melodies of the songs of the gandharvas.

Salutation to that Buddha, the protector of the earth who, upon his birth, caused the entire abode of the three worlds to tremble; to him, the omniscient one whose all-pervading movements have ceased.
A sutra was spoken by the Blessed One.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered Śrāvastī for alms.
Having walked through Śrāvastī for alms in regular order, he went to where the young brahmin Śuka, son of Taudeya, was.

He approached that residence. Now at that time, in the residence of the young brahmin Śuka, the son of Taudeya, the elephant Śaṅkhakuñjara was seated upon a couch covered with a woolen rug. He was eating rice and meat porridge from a bronze bowl with a stone lid. The Blessed One saw the elephant Śaṅkhakuñjara seated upon the couch covered with the woolen rug.

He saw the Blessed One eating from a bronze bowl with a stone lid. Śaṅkhakuñjara went to the threshold of the door and bellowed again. Then the Blessed One said this to Śaṅkhakuñjara: "Śaṅkha, even this does not tame your mind, since you have gone from making the sound 'bhokāra' to bellowing. When this was said, Śaṅkhakuñjara—

With his anger intensified, having become fierce and displeased, he descended from the couch covered with a woolen rug and sat down on a wooden bench beneath the couch. Now at that time, the young brahmin Śuka, the son of Taudeya, had gone out on some business. Then the young brahmin Śuka, the son of Taudeya, returned. The young brahmin Śuka, the son of Taudeya, saw him.

Śaṅkhakuñjara had fallen down beneath a wooden trough. Seeing this, he addressed the people: "Who has said anything to you regarding Śaṅkhakuñjara? Who among us would say anything to my son Śaṅkhakuñjara? However, the ascetic Gautama has arrived; standing at the threshold of the door, he bellows in this manner. To him, the ascetic Gautama said: "This too is for you, Śaṅkha..."
"You do not tame yourself, since you have gone from making the sound *bho* to making the sound *bukka*. When this was said, Śaṅkhakuñjara became exceedingly angry, fierce, and displeased;
he descended from his couch covered with a woolen rug and sat down beneath the couch on a wooden drain-pipe. Then Śuka— (croaked)—

Afflicted, enraged, furious, and displeased, he departed from his woolen carpet and went toward the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada. Now at that time, the Blessed One was seated before an assembly of many hundreds of monks, teaching the Dharma. The Blessed One saw the young brahmin Śuka, the son of Taudeya, approaching from afar.

Having seen him, he addressed the monks again: "Monks, do you see the young brahmin Śuka, son of Taudeya, coming this very way? "Yes, Venerable Sir. "If the young brahmin Śuka, son of Taudeya, were to die at this moment, then upon the breakup of the body after death, he would fall into a state of misery, a bad destination, and perdition, just like an arrow shot [straight down]."

"He would be reborn in the *vicikitsā* hell. For in this way, his mind was corrupted in my presence. Because of that corruption of mind as the cause, such beings here, upon the dissolution of the body after death, are reborn in states of woe, in miserable destinies, in the Avīci hell.
Then, at that time, a certain monk spoke this verse:"
Having seen a certain person here with a corrupted mind,
the Teacher explained this matter in the midst of the assembly of monks:
"Alas, let the young man now pass away without distraction!"
One would be reborn in the hells, for the mind has been corrupted by this.
Just as [an object] thrown down according to its nature, even so do sentient beings go to an evil destination because of the cause of corrupting their minds toward the Tathāgata.
The young brahmin Taudeyaputra, wishing to revile [the Buddha], approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he exchanged various pleasant and courteous greetings with the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Once seated, the young brahmin Taudeyaputra Śuka addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Has the Blessed One Gautama arrived?"
"This is our residence. Upon his arrival, the Blessed One Gautama said something to Śaṅkhakuñjara:
'In this place, young man, having dressed in the forenoon and taken my bowl and robe, I entered Śrāvastī for alms.
Having completed my alms-round through Śrāvastī, I approached your residence here. Having approached..."
I was standing at the foot of the gate. At that time, the elephant Śaṅkhakuñjara had mounted a couch spread with a woolen rug and was eating rice and meat from a bronze bowl with an iron lid.
Seeing me standing at the foot of the gate, Śaṅkhakuñjara trumpeted. When he saw me, I said this to him:

"Even this, Śaṅkha, does not humble you: that you have gone from saying 'Bho' to bellowing like a bull. When this was said, Śaṅkhakuñjara became resentful, angry, fierce, and displeased; he descended from the couch covered with a woolen rug and sat down beneath the couch in the wooden drain. "How could the Blessed Gautama possibly know of our past [deeds], Śaṅkhakuñjara?"

"He knows what has been born. Enough, young man, stay! Do not question him about this matter; it will result in resentment, intolerance, and mental distress for you. For a second and even a third time, the young brahmin Śuka, son of Taudeya, said this to the Blessed One: "Does the Blessed Gautama indeed recognize our Śaṅkhakuñjara as having been born in a previous life?"

"Enough, young man! Stop! Do not question me on this matter. Otherwise, you will experience resentment, impatience, and mental distress right here and now. You are not fit for this, young man. [He said this] up to a second and even a third time.
"Listen, young man; attend well and thoroughly to what I shall say. I will speak to you, young man. [That which is yours, young man...]
"Your father, a descendant of Todeya—he has been reborn in a low birth as a dog after the dissolution of his body.

'But, Master Gautama, it will be thus: our father, who performed sacrifices, maintained the sacred fires, and raised the sacrificial posts, will, upon the dissolution of his body, be reborn in the radiant Brahma-world. It is because of this very pride and arrogance of yours, young man, that your father..."

"Taudeya, the great lord of donors, has been reborn in the womb of a dog. Young man, if you do not believe what I have said to you, then, young man, go to your own residence. Having arrived there, speak thus to Śaṅkhakuñjara: 'If you, Śaṅkhakuñjara, were our father in a previous birth, namely Taudeya...'"
"Ascend the couch covered with a woolen rug. Once you have ascended, speak thus:

'If you, Śaṅkhakuñjara, were our father Taudeya in a former birth, may you enjoy this! May you eat rice and meat porridge from a bronze bowl with a stone slab as a cushion. When he has finished eating, say to him: 'If you...'"
"Śaṅkhakuñjara was our father in a former birth; he was Taudeya. Since you did not point out my existing wealth to us at the time of our death, please point it out now. "I shall point it out.
Then the young brahmin Śuka, son of Taudeya, having received and mastered what was spoken by the Blessed One, went to his own [home].

He approached that residence. Having approached, he said this to Śaṅkhakuñjara: "If you, Śaṅkhakuñjara, were our father Taudeya in a former birth, then mount [this couch]. When he had mounted the couch spread with woolen rugs, he addressed him thus: "If you, Śaṅkhakuñjara, were our father in a former birth..."
"Your father Taudeya used to eat rice and meat with boiled milk in a bronze bowl with an iron stand; you should do the same.

He ate it. When he had finished eating, [Śāriputra] said this to him: "If you, Śaṅkhakuñjara, were our father Taudeya in a previous birth, then regarding my own property that existed at the time of my death—"

"Show that which has not been shown. Then Śaṅkhakuñjara descended from his couch covered with a woolen rug and approached a certain old dwelling-house. Having arrived there, he sniffed with his snout at four foot-stools for the couch and the center of the floor marked by his own hoof-prints. Thereupon, the young brahmin Śuka, the son of Taudeya, [took] the gold and bullion that had been worked and unworked...
He acquired four iron trunks and, from their center, a golden water-pot.
Then the young brahmin Śuka, son of Taudeya, having hidden that gold, became joyful, satisfied, elated, and filled with gladness;
he departed from Śrāvastī and approached the Blessed One. Now at that time, the Blessed One...

Seated before an assembly of several hundred monks, he was teaching the Dharma. The Blessed One saw the young brahmin Śuka, the son of Taudeya, approaching from afar, and having seen him, he addressed the monks: "Monks, do you see the young brahmin Śuka, the son of Taudeya, approaching from afar?"

"So it is, Venerable Sir. If Śuka Māṇava, the son of Taudeya, were to die at this very moment, he would, upon the breaking up of the body, be reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly worlds, just like an arrow shot [straight]. For he has cleared his mind toward me. Monks, it is because of the clearing of the mind that some beings here, upon the breaking up of the body..."
They are reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly worlds. Then, at that time, a certain monk spoke this verse:
"Having seen a certain person here with a serene mind, the Teacher explained this matter in the midst of the assembly of monks."
Now, this man, having abandoned his faults, should meet his end;
with a mind purified, he will be reborn among the gods.
Just as evil has been cast away, so too is it with the Tathāgata.
"By reason of the clarity of their minds, sentient beings go to a good destination.
Then the young brahmin Śuka, son of Taudeya, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

To the young Śuka, son of Taudeya, as he was thus seated, the Blessed One said this: "Young man, is it exactly as I have prophesied regarding Śaṅkhakuñjara? "O Gautama, it is exactly so; it is just as the Blessed Gautama has prophesied concerning Śaṅkhakuñjara. Furthermore, we would ask the Blessed Gautama something else."
"If you would grant me the opportunity, I shall provide an opening for the answering of your question. Ask me, young man, whatever you desire to know.

"Venerable Gautama, what is the cause, what is the condition, by which some beings here are short-lived and others long-lived; some are afflicted with many ailments and others with few ailments; some are ill-favored and others well-favored; some are of little renown and others of great renown; and some are born into low families..."

"Furthermore, some are of high birth while others are not; some have speech that is not authoritative while others have authoritative speech; some have little wealth while others have great wealth; some are of weak wisdom while others are of great wisdom. Reverend Gautama, by the ripening of what karma is this diversity among sentient beings perceived?

Thereupon, the Blessed One said this to the young brahmin Śuka, the son of Taudeya: "Young man, I shall teach you the Dharma discourse called the *Karmavibhaṅga* (The Analysis of Karma). Therefore..."

"Listen well and attend thoroughly; I shall speak. "So be it, Blessed One," the young brahmin Śuka, son of Taudeya, replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: "Young man, I say that beings are owners of their actions, heirs of their actions, born of their actions, and have their actions as their refuge. It is action, young man, that divides beings, namely—"

Regarding inferiority, superiority, and mediocrity: for example, there is karma that leads to a short lifespan; there is karma that leads to a long lifespan. There is karma that leads to much affliction; there is karma that leads to little affliction. There is karma that leads to an ugly complexion; there is karma that leads to a beautiful appearance. There is karma that leads to being of little renown; there is karma that leads to being of great renown. There is karma that leads to rebirth in a low family; there is karma that leads to [rebirth in] a high family.

Rebirth in a high family; rebirth in a low family; rebirth with little wealth; rebirth with great wealth; rebirth with poor wisdom; rebirth with great wisdom; rebirth in hell; rebirth in the animal realm; rebirth in the world of hungry ghosts; rebirth in the world of asuras; rebirth in the world of humans; rebirth among the gods of the desire realm; rebirth among the gods of the form realm.

a. k. Rebirth among the gods of the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*). a. k. [Karma] that is performed but not accumulated (*kṛtaṃ nopacitam*). a. k. [Karma] that is accumulated but not performed (*upacitaṃ na kṛtam*). a. k. [Karma] that is both performed and accumulated (*kṛtam upacitaṃ ca*). a. k. [Karma] that is neither performed nor accumulated (*naiva kṛtaṃ nopacitam*). a. k. That [karma] endowed with which a person, having been reborn in the hells, passes away after exhausting the full lifespan of a hell-being. a. k. That [karma] endowed with which...
A person born in the hells passes away after having exhausted the full lifespan of a denizen of hell.

Some pass away immediately upon being born in the hells. Some have a certain rebirth; some have an uncertain rebirth. Some have a counteractive force against other regions. Some, having previously been happy, later become miserable.

a. k. y. s. p. Having been miserable previously, one becomes happy later. a. k. y. s. p. Having been happy previously, one becomes happy later. a. k. y. s. p. Having been miserable previously, one becomes miserable later. a. k. (MKV 31)
One who has performed both wholesome and unwholesome actions becomes wealthy yet stingy. One who has performed unwholesome actions and not wholesome ones becomes poor yet generous.

One who has performed wholesome actions and not unwholesome ones becomes wealthy and generous. There is a person whose karma is exhausted but not their lifespan; there is a person whose lifespan is exhausted but not their karma; and there is one for whom both lifespan and karma are exhausted.

a. p. y. One whose lifespan is exhausted and whose merits are also exhausted. a. p. y. One whose lifespan is not exhausted and whose karma is not [exhausted], but rather whose afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted. a. p. One who is happy in body but not in mind. a. p. One who is happy in mind but not in body. a. p. One who is happy both in body and in mind. a. p. One who is happy neither in body nor in mind. a. k. y. s. Such a person (*pudgala*).

A person who has performed actions leading to rebirth in the miserable states (*apāya*) that are conducive to beauty, when born in the miserable states, is handsome, with a supple body and smooth skin; they are pleasing to the eye and beautiful to behold.

A person who has performed actions leading to rebirth in the miserable states that are conducive to ugliness, when born in the miserable states, is ill-favored in color, with a coarse body, terrible to behold, and repulsive to behold.

A person who has performed actions leading to rebirth in the miserable states that are conducive to defects in the faculties, when born in the miserable states, is foul-smelling, with crooked faculties and indistinct faculties.

Through the ripening of the ten unwholesome paths of action, the increase of ten external phenomena is perceived. Through the ripening of the ten wholesome paths of action, the decline of ten external phenomena is perceived.
There are ten benefits of joining one’s palms in reverence at a Tathāgata’s shrine. There are ten benefits of venerating a Tathāgata’s shrine.
There are ten benefits of giving an umbrella. There are ten benefits of giving a bell. There are ten benefits of giving clothing.

There are ten benefits of giving a seat. There are ten benefits of giving a vessel. There are ten benefits of giving food. There are ten benefits of giving a vehicle. There are ten benefits of giving shelter. There are ten benefits of giving a drink.
There are ten benefits in the bestowing of fruits. There are ten benefits in the bestowing of garlands. There are ten benefits in the bestowing of loose flowers.

There are ten benefits in the bestowing of lamps. There are ten benefits in the bestowing of perfumes. (MKV 32) There are ten benefits in going forth. There are ten benefits in dwelling in the forest. There are ten benefits in being an alms-food eater. There are ten grounds of self-confidence.
This is the summary of the Dharma discourse on the Analysis of Karma.

I. In this regard, what is the karma that leads to a short lifespan? It is said: killing living beings; rejoicing in the killing of living beings; speaking in praise of the killing of living beings; and delighting in the death of enemies.

Inciting others to the death of enemies; praising the death of enemies; causing abortion; praising the causing of abortion; establishing sacrificial altars where many living beings—such as buffaloes, cattle, pigs, and chickens—are slaughtered;
and the sons, grandsons, and other people of that one who initiates such sacrifices, seeking rewards and driven by fear, following after him.
While performing [such acts], they destroy sentient beings.
For example, it is said that in the great city of Kāśmīra, a certain monk who was an Arhat was standing at the door of a house.
Alongside that house ran a royal road, and by it an animal was being led along while bleating. When that monk saw it, he—
"Alas! Woe! What misery! he cried out. The men asked him, "Noble sir, what is this sound of 'Alas! Woe! What misery!'?

He replied, "This must not be told to those who lack faith; however, for the sake of the matter at hand, I shall speak. This animal being led away while bleating—formerly, when this man was a lord of merchants, he established an altar (*sthaṇḍila*) for the annual [sacrifice]."

And he established the animal sacrifice. Therein, many animals were slaughtered by him. At the time of his death, he summoned his sons and said: "Sons, if you have any affection for me, this annual animal sacrifice which has been established by me must be continued after I have passed away. His sons promised, "So be it. He then passed away.

Endowed with that killing born of delusion, he was reborn as a beast in his own home. There, in birth after birth, he was slaughtered; now, for the sixty-first time, he is being led away. Then, feeling compassion for that beast, the monk said: "The sacrificial ground is yours alone."

The sacrifice was performed by you yourself; many animals were slaughtered. Why do you roar? All of this is meaningless—such as the preparation of this sacrificial ground, as well as the witnessing of battle, wherein many beings, including elephants, horses, and men, are slain, and the rejoicing in weapons associated with war.

c) And as it was said by the Blessed One in the *Kālika-sūtra* at Vaiśālī: "Ānanda, the taking of life, when practiced and frequently cultivated, leads to rebirth in hell; it also leads to rebirth in the animal realm, and it also leads to rebirth in the domain of hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, because even a small act of taking life has a ripening result, for one who has become a human being, it leads to a short lifespan."
d) Likewise, ten disadvantages of taking life are stated in the *Nandika-sūtra*.
This action leads to a short lifespan.
II. In that regard, what is the action that leads to a long lifespan? It is said: abstaining from taking life. Upon abstaining from taking life...

Speaking in praise [of others]. Encouraging them therein. Speaking in praise of that. Liberating humans, cattle, pigs, chickens, and so forth who have been condemned to death. Granting fearlessness to terrified beings.
Having a mind of compassion among beings who are without a protector. Having a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward sick beings.
And [giving] to others, such as the young and the old; providing them with food; maintaining a mind of loving-kindness toward those who receive [gifts];

and that which was previously mentioned regarding the side of virtue, such as witnessing battles and so forth; likewise, the restoration of ruined stūpas, caityas, and monasteries. For this very reason it has been said:
There shall be no untimely death for one who repairs what is broken or shattered.
Likewise, they describe the *Baka-pratyeka-brahmasūtra*. It is said that by him, having become a seer (*ṛṣi*) endowed with the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), [this was accomplished].
For a caravan afflicted by thirst that had strayed from the path, a rain was brought down by means of supernatural power. And for that purpose, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"I remember here, having awakened from sleep, that ancient vow, conduct, and observance of yours."
And in that caravan, there was a Bodhisattva who served as the caravan leader.
He was the one who had been captured on the bank of the Eṇī river.
The Eṇī is the name of a river, along whose bank a certain king had been seized by an enemy.

Having entered the Himavat mountains, he was led away and captured as one condemned to death, along with his army and vehicles. By that man who had become a seer, a wind and rain were released through supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). And by means of a stratagem, the host of enemy people was thrown into confusion.
That king was liberated. This is your second instance of conduct in the observance of vows and moral discipline.
Awakened from sleep, I remember this:
that king was a Bodhisattva,
and his boat was seized by the current of the Ganges.

By a fierce and powerful nāga, that rishi—who was then possessed of great supernatural power and the five superknowledges—was dwelling on the bank of the Gaṅgā; by him, your body, which was crying out and despairing of life, was liberated from that [danger]. This is your third observance of vows and conduct.
Having awakened from my dream, I recall that at that time the Bodhisattva was the master of that ship. You performed such threefold karma;
therefore, you have become exceedingly long-lived.

b) As some teachers relate: The Blessed One said, "In the past, monks, a pestilence afflicted all the inhabited regions of Jambudvīpa. Then, a certain being residing in another world-system heard from a person possessed of supernatural powers that the pestilence had been brought to an end in Jambudvīpa. Having performed meritorious deeds, he made this aspiration. (MKV 36)
"May I be reborn in Jambudvīpa for the sake of destroying the diseases of all sentient beings. He was reborn there.

For those sentient beings who were thirsty, he destroyed their disease with drink; for those who were hungry, he destroyed their disease with food. In this way, whatever was needed by whichever being, with that very thing he destroyed their disease. Indeed, it was not [otherwise] for him...

There was not even the slightest thing that was not medicine; whatever he took and gave was itself a medicine. Therefore, the humans of Jambudvīpa gave it the single name "All-Medicine" (Sarvauṣadhi). Then, monks, the physician-king Sarvauṣadhi, having granted life to many thousands of beings, passed away. After some time, he was reborn in a royal family in Mithilā.
Then, having become Mahādeva, he caused eighty thousand kṣatriyas to go forth [into homelessness] through his teaching of the Dharma.

In Jambudvīpa, the lifespan of humans remained at eighty thousand years and did not diminish. Passing away from there after some time, he became Māndhātṛ in the city of Kuśinagarī. Furthermore, during the teaching of the seven suns...
The manava named Sunetra is to be known as me, monks; at that time, I was Sarvauṣadhivaidyarāja.

By the ripening of that karma, the lifespan of Mahādeva is to be calculated [as equal to mine]; the lifespan of both Māndhātṛ and Sunetra is likewise to be calculated in this same way. This is the karma that leads to long life.

III. What is the action that leads to much affliction? It is said: giving blows with the fist or the open hand; rejoicing in the giving of blows with the fist or the open hand; praising the giving of blows with the fist or the open hand; feeling satisfaction in their being given; causing pain to the mind or body of one's mother and father;
likewise, causing mental defilement in other virtuous renunciants; and feeling satisfaction in the illness of an enemy.

Dissatisfaction arising from the emergence of enemies or diseases; providing no medicine to those who are ill; likewise, consuming food that has not been properly digested—this is the action that leads to much affliction. IV. What is the action that leads to little affliction? It is said: abstaining from striking with the fist or the open hand. In that regard:

Encouraging others [to practice virtue], speaking in praise of that, and rejoicing in it; attending to sick parents, as well as other householders and renunciants; being glad at heart when they are afflicted by enemies or disease, and glad at heart when they recover from it; providing medicine, and giving food that is easily digested—this is the action that leads to having little illness.

V. What is the action that leads to an ugly complexion? It is said: anger, enmity, hypocrisy, spite; speaking ill of one’s mother and father; [speaking ill] of others—whether householders or renunciants, whether young or old; failing to clean the ground around a stūpa, a courtyard, a shrine, or a monastery;
extinguishing the lamps at stūpas or images; mocking beings who are of ugly appearance; and likewise, being habitually fastidious about cleanliness.
This action leads to an ugly complexion. VI.

What kind of action leads to a beautiful appearance? It is said: freedom from anger; freedom from malice; freedom from hypocrisy; the gift of clothing; the application of plaster to stūpas and shrines; the gift of golden vessels; and the gift of fragrant ointments.
Giving ornaments; speaking in praise of one's mother and father; speaking in praise of the noble ones who possess virtuous conduct; sweeping the courtyards of stūpas and monasteries;
constantly sweeping one’s own home; not mocking beings who are deformed, nor others such as children and the elderly; and likewise, maintaining clean habits in one’s conduct.

a) For example, it is said that when the noble Sundarananda performed a steam-bath (*jentāka-snāna*) for the community of monks during the time of the Perfectly Awakened One Krakucchanda, his mind was filled with serene faith upon seeing them. Furthermore, he applied a coating of gold and yellow orpiment to the stūpa of a pratyekabuddha;
having seen this as well, his mind was again filled with serene faith, and he dedicated [the merit] toward physical beauty. Moreover—
And while the stūpa was being constructed, he had the first parasol made. Just as he himself prophesied in his final existence:
"Through bathing with *jentāka* [fragrant water], through anointing with yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), and through the gift of a single parasol, I have attained this golden complexion."

In that very way, this one has shone. This action leads to being pleasing to behold. VII. What is the action that leads to being called "of little power"? It is said: envy; stinginess; dissatisfaction with another’s gain;
dissatisfaction with another’s praise; contempt for one’s mother and father; and contempt for noble ones who possess virtuous conduct.

Likewise, [speaking ill] of others who are sick, young, or old; praising that which is inferior, devoid of Dharma, or rooted in unwholesomeness; obstructing the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); and rejoicing in such acts—this is the karma that leads to being known as one of little power. VIII. What is the karma that leads to being known as one of great power? It is said: freedom from envy, freedom from stinginess, and [rejoicing] in the gains of others.

Contentment. Contentment upon hearing the renown, praise, fame, and verses concerning another. Taking joy in the speaking of another's virtues. Having shrines and stūpas constructed for the Blessed One. Preventing [others] from inferior states, from the lack of Dharma, and from unwholesome roots. Encouraging others toward great and powerful wholesome roots.
Arousing the thought of awakening (bodhicitta). Arousing the thought of awakening toward all great and powerful wholesome roots.

a) As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Pūrvāparāntaka-sūtra* at Vārāṇasī (MKV 40): "Ajita, the Bodhisattva has been exhorted. Indeed, Ajita, your mind is being tamed for a great eagerness, namely, for the sake of causing the Saṅgha to decline. For it will be said: 'Maitreya, however, dwells in the Tuṣita abode of the gods.'"

May he by whom worship is to be obtained in heaven, on earth, and here [in this world], having swiftly attained the state of the Ten Powers, become eternally worthy of worship by the worlds like the moon.
This is the action that leads to being of great renown. IX.
What is the action that leads to birth in a low family? It is said: arrogance; conceit; lack of filial respect toward one’s mother and father;

lack of respect for ascetics (*śramaṇa*); lack of respect for brahmins (*brāhmaṇa*); failure to honor the elders of the family; failing to attend upon one’s mother and father; [and failing to attend upon] the noble ones (*ārya*).
Not attending upon those who possess virtuous conduct; not attending upon others who occupy the position of gurus, such as teachers and preceptors;

and showing contempt for beings born into low families—this is the karma that leads to birth in a low family. What is the karma that leads to birth in a high family? It is said: freedom from arrogance, absence of conceit, and knowing how to honor one’s mother and father.

The state of being a śramaṇa; the state of being a brahmin; honoring the elders of the family; attending upon one's mother and father; attending upon noble and virtuous persons; attending upon other teachers and preceptors who occupy the position of gurus;
and not despising beings born into lowly families.

a) And as it was said by the Blessed One in a sūtra: "Monks, when ordained ones who possess virtuous conduct, lead a holy life, and are endowed with wholesome qualities approach, five benefits are to be expected for that family. What are the five? Here, monks, when those possessing virtuous conduct have approached, they gladden their minds; this leads to rebirth in heaven. (MKV 41)

Monks, at that time, that family has entered upon the path. Furthermore, monks, when those who are virtuous approach, they greet them and rise to meet them; monks, this is the path leading to rebirth in a high family, which at that time has been entered upon. In this manner, the entire sūtra is to be applied. This is the karma.
[This leads to] birth in a high family. XI.
What is the action that leads to having few possessions? It is said: taking what is not given; inciting others to take what is not given;

speaking in praise of theft; rejoicing in such acts; cutting off the livelihood of one's mother and father; and likewise [cutting off the livelihood] of others who are sick, children, the elderly, or miserable.

The interruption of livelihood; lack of contentment with the gains of others; creating obstacles to the gains of others; and rejoicing in famine—this is the karma that leads to meager possessions. XII. In this regard, what is the karma that leads to great possessions? It is said: abstaining from taking what is not given from others...
Abstaining from taking what is not given; rejoicing in others who have desisted from taking what is not given; providing for the livelihood of one's mother and father;
providing for the livelihood of noble and virtuous persons; likewise, providing for the livelihood of others who are sick, young, old, or miserable;
being satisfied by another’s gain; being dissatisfied by another’s loss; rejoicing in another’s gain; and delighting in abundance.

a) That same sutra should be applied here. Furthermore, monks, when those who possess virtue have approached, people give gifts and perform meritorious deeds. At that time, monks, that family has entered upon the practice that leads to great wealth. This is the karma that leads to great wealth.

XIII. In this regard, what is the action that leads to a lack of wisdom? It is said: here, a certain person does not question others—the wise, the ascetics, or the brahmins—asking, "What is the Dharma? What Dharma brings about the highest good for one who practices it? Instead, he associates with those of poor wisdom and avoids the wise; he illuminates false teachings and reviles the true Dharma.

He cuts off the confidence of the preachers of the true Dharma. Out of attachment, he does not offer words of praise to the preachers of the true Dharma, yet he offers words of praise to the preachers of the false Dharma. He extols wrong view and disparages right view. Likewise, he cuts off the livelihood of those who copy, read, or recite the scriptures.

a) And it is said in the Sūtra: "One performs actions leading to madness; one dies deluded and becomes one of poor wisdom. As stated in the Nandika-sūtra, thirty-five disadvantages are to be applied to the occasion of negligence through fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants. One becomes disrespectful toward the Buddha, and one becomes disrespectful toward the Dharma and the Saṅgha. Therefore, [this refers to] the Śākya-sūtra.

It should be connected [to the previous context]. And when the Blessed One arrived at Kapilavastu, that Śākya, due to the fault of drinking intoxicants, never approached the Blessed One. He was converted by four elders sent by the Blessed One, and he passed away.
A Śākya asked: "Blessed One, what is his destination? The Blessed One said: "Even these Śākyas of mine..."

The Sūtra should be applied thus: "They may understand the meaning of what has been spoken. For example, there was a monk named Cūḍapanthaka who lived in Rājagṛha; the Blessed One recited a verse to him, yet at the end of the rainy season retreat he was unable to master it. The monks, filled with wonder, asked [the Buddha].

"Blessed One, as the ripening of what karma is he so lacking in wisdom? The Blessed One said: "After the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa had passed into parinirvāṇa, this monk lived in the forest and was a master of the Tripiṭaka at that time. While the monks were not performing worship to the Buddha, the Buddha’s word disappeared. Those monks went into his presence and said, 'The Buddha’s word for us... "

"It has disappeared. Give us instruction as well. Because of this fault of stinginess, he did not give them instruction. Thus that teaching disappeared. Through the ripening of that karma, he is one of poor wisdom; this karma leads to poor wisdom. XIV. In that regard, what is the karma that leads to great wisdom? It is said: (MKV 44)
In this case, a certain person is of an inquisitive nature; he attends upon wise śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas and avoids those of poor wisdom.

He illuminates the true Dharma and censures what is not the true Dharma. He praises the confidence of the preachers of the Dharma, gives applause to those who speak coherently, and avoids those who speak incoherently. [He upholds] right view...

He describes [this]. He censures wrong view. He gives gifts of ink, books, and pens. And he does not drink liquor. As it is said in the Nandika-sūtra: "The thirty-five faults of drinking liquor are to be associated with the unwholesome side. This action leads to great wisdom.

XV. In this regard, what is the action that leads to rebirth in hell? It is said: the intense misdeeds of body, speech, and mind committed by one with a thoroughly corrupt mind; the view of annihilationism; the view of eternalism; the nihilistic view; the view of non-action; the doctrine of stinginess; ingratitude; the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*); and the giving of false accusations against the virtuous noble ones. This is it.
Karma that leads to rebirth in hell.
XVI. In this regard, what is the karma that leads to rebirth in the animal realm? It is said: it is intermediate misconduct of body, speech, and mind;
various actions arising from passion, various actions arising from hatred, and various actions arising from delusion.
Karma: giving what is improper to one's parents or to those who have gone forth; mocking sentient beings who have been born as animals;
and likewise, the karma of a vow, such as the vow of those who observe the "cow-vow" or the "dog-vow," thinking, "May I be reborn here.
(a) Furthermore, the *avadāna* from the *Siṃhajātaka* of the Bodhisattva should be told, as well as the case of the Brahmin Varṣākāra being reborn as a monkey. For example: (MKV 45)

The brahmin Varṣākāra saw the elder monk Mahākāśyapa traveling through the air from Vulture Peak Mountain toward the side of Ṛṣigiri. With a malicious mind, due to his association with Devadatta and Ajātaśatru, he committed a verbal transgression, saying: "This śramaṇa, as he travels through the air, goes from mountain to mountain; it is just like this: [and so forth].

The monkey went from tree to tree. The Blessed One said: "By the brahmin Varṣākāra, having become angry, verbal misconduct was committed. What is its ripening? The Blessed One replied: "As the ripening of this verbal misconduct, the brahmin Varṣākāra will become a monkey for five hundred future births. Then, by that Varṣākāra...

The Blessed One had indeed declared that he would become a monkey for five hundred future births. With a mind filled with agitation, he developed faith; therefore, at the time of the Blessed One’s final nirvana, he asked: "When will the exhaustion of that karma occur? The Blessed One said: "It will be those same five hundred future births, but in Rājagṛha."
"You will be reborn just as one is born from a rose-apple tree (*jambu*) in Jambudvīpa—where there are fruits the size of camels—and with a flavor like pure, honey-like nectar.

There you will take birth; having emerged from that state, you will attain a happy rebirth, such as being born among lions due to the corruption of your mind. And for that purpose, a verse was spoken by the Blessed One."
Long is the night for one who stays awake; long is the league for one who is weary;
long is saṃsāra for the fool who does not understand the true Dharma.
This action leads to rebirth in the animal realm.

XVII. In this regard, what is the action that leads to rebirth in the world of Yama? It is said: the misconduct of body, speech, and mind of one who is angry and whose mind is hostile; greed, dishonest greed, and wrong livelihood; the death of one who is angry, hungry, and thirsty; and the death of one whose mind is attached to material things.
a) As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* within the *Śatavarga-āgama*:

"Furthermore, Ānanda, for that person, either karma performed in another birth has presented itself, or at the time of death there is a wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). This karma leads to rebirth in the world of Yama. XVIII. In this regard, what is the karma that leads to rebirth in the world of the asuras? It is said: all mild misconduct of body, speech, and mind.

Pride (*māna*), overweening pride (*abhimāna*), excessive pride (*adhimāna*), the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*), and false pride (*mithyāmāna*). When the roots of wholesome merit are dedicated toward rebirth in the world of the *asuras*, and when immorality arises from the most intense passion through the gateway of wisdom—this is the karma that leads to rebirth in the world of the *asuras*.
XIX. In this regard, what is the karma that leads to rebirth in the world of humans? It is said: [actions] well-cultivated and weakly cultivated.

And there are ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa kuśalāḥ karmapathāḥ*). Which ten? Threefold bodily action, fourfold verbal action, and threefold mental action. This [set of] karma leads to rebirth in the human world. XX.

In that regard, what is the karma that leads to rebirth among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*)? It is said: the ten wholesome paths of action when fully perfected—this karma leads to rebirth among the gods of the desire realm.

XXI. In this regard, what is the karma that leads to rebirth among the gods of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*)? It is said: the ten paths of wholesome action (*kuśala-karmapatha*) that are well-perfected, well-concentrated, more distinguished than those [of the desire realm], and complete. This is the karma that leads to rebirth among the gods of the form realm. XXII. In this regard, what is the karma that leads to rebirth among the gods of the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*)? It is said: the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

The sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—when these meditative attainments have been cultivated and practiced extensively, this constitutes the karma that leads to rebirth among the gods of the formless realm. XXIII. In this regard, what is karma that has been performed but not accumulated? It is said: that karma which, having been performed, one regrets, feels ashamed of, censures, loathes, confesses, declares, and makes manifest. (Madhyamakakārikāvṛtti)
One undertakes restraint for the future and does not perform [the action] again. This action is performed but not accumulated.

XXIV. In that regard, what is an action that is accumulated but not performed? It is said: an action that ought to be fulfilled by means of the body, yet one speaks with a corrupted mind, saying, "I shall do this to you"—this action is accumulated but not performed.
XXV. In this regard, what is action that is both performed and accumulated? It is said: it is intentional action (*sāṃcetanika*).
As the Blessed One has stated:
"Mental states are preceded by the mind, have the mind as their chief, and are swift as the mind."
If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind,
then suffering follows him, even as the wheel follows the hoof of the draught-ox.
Mental states are preceded by the mind, have the mind as their chief, and are made of the mind.
If one speaks or acts with a serene mind, happiness follows that person like a shadow that never departs.
This is the deed performed and accumulated.

XXVI. In that regard, what is action that is neither performed nor accumulated? It is said: action that is intentional (*sāṃcetanika*) but performed or caused to be performed within a dream. This action is neither performed nor accumulated. XXVII. In that regard, what is the action endowed with which a person, having been reborn in the hells, passes away only after exhausting the full lifespan of a hell-being? It is said: here, a certain person has performed and accumulated an action pertaining to the hells. Having performed that action, he does not experience [its result immediately].

He does not feel shame, he does not reproach himself, he does not loathe it, he does not confess it, he does not declare it, he does not reveal it, nor does he undertake restraint for the future; rather, he rejoices all the more and gives rise to delight, just as Devadatta, Kokālika, and others did.
This is the karma endowed with which a person, having been reborn in the hells, passes away only after exhausting a full lifespan of a hell-being.

XXVIII. In this regard, what is that karma endowed with which a person, having been reborn in the hells, passes away after exhausting half of the hellish lifespan? It is said: Here, a certain person has performed and accumulated karma leading to the hells. Having committed it, he does not feel remorse, he is not ashamed, he does not reproach himself, he does not loathe it, he does not confess it, and he does not reveal it.

He does not manifest it, nor does he undertake restraint for the future; rather, he does not rejoice with greater intensity, nor does he produce joy. A person endowed with this karma, having been reborn in the hells, passes away after exhausting half of the lifespan of the hell-dwellers.
XXIX. In this regard, what is the karma endowed with which a person, as soon as they are reborn in the hells, passes away?

It is said: Here, a certain person has performed and accumulated hellish karma. Having performed it, he feels remorse; he is ashamed, he censures it, he loathes it, he confesses it, he reveals it, he makes it manifest, and he undertakes restraint for the future.

He incurs [the offense], but does not carry it out again. If he is reborn in the hells, he passes away immediately upon being reborn—just as King Ajātaśatru did. With Devadatta as his accomplice, he committed acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*): the murder of his father, the schism of the Saṅgha, the release of Dhanapāla, and by Devadatta’s command, the release of the stone-mechanism. Because of that, he went to the Avīci hell.

Having heard this, he became deeply moved and developed serene faith toward the Blessed One. In the *Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra*, he confessed his transgressions and reconnected with his roots of virtue. At the time of death, he maintained a serene mind; even with his bones, he [honored] the Buddha, the Blessed One.

"I go for refuge. He passes away immediately upon being reborn. This is the karma endowed with which a person passes away immediately upon being reborn in the hells. XXX. In that regard, what is the karma that leads to certain rebirth? It is said: having performed [an action], one dedicates it toward a specific rebirth, thinking, "May I be reborn there. One is then reborn there. Just as in the Jātaka tales of the Blessed One, such as the Śyāmāka-jātaka and others, rebirth is described as occurring by the power of a vow (*praṇidhāna*). This is the karma that leads to certain rebirth.

XXXI. In this regard, what is action that leads to birth in an indefinite state? It is said: that which, having been performed, one does not dedicate toward any specific rebirth, thinking, "May I be born there. Just as sentient beings are born by the power of karma, such is action that leads to birth in an indefinite state.

XXXII. In this regard, what is called "karma that ripens in another place"? It is that karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome—which ripens for one who has gone to another place, either in that very life or in a subsequent birth. That is karma that ripens in another place. As the Blessed One said: "In the past, monks, the lifespan of humans in Jambudvīpa was immeasurable."

As in the case of King Māndhātṛ. Now, in a certain city, there was a son of a caravan leader named Maitrāyajña. Surrounded by five hundred companions, he went to a park. And those companions said to him: "In this city, the merchants, having placed your father at their head, have descended into the great ocean."

"Having gone to other countries such as Suvarṇabhūmi and having seen other islands, they acquire wealth. We too, making you our leader, shall descend upon the ocean, acquire wealth, and see other islands. Then he promised, "So be it. Having gone at night, he [approached] his mother...

He took leave, saying, "Mother, we shall go to Suvarṇabhūmi. His mother said, "Son, immeasurable wealth remains in the house; you must not go. At his mother's word, he turned back. He went to the park again, and his companions said to him, "Let us inform him of this matter. He consented, saying, "So be it. He went there once more...
He went to his mother and asked her permission. Again, he was turned back by his mother through prostrating at her feet. This happened a third time as well.
After some time, having gone to the park again, he was told by his companions: "Because of your fault, we too shall not go. Let us ask [her]."
"Tomorrow, on the thirteenth day, we shall depart. Without his mother's knowledge, he had already sent out a great deal of merchandise.

As he was setting out at the time of departure, his mother stood at the door, falling at his feet and saying, "Son, you must not go! Enraged, he placed his foot upon his mother's head and passed her by, eventually reaching the shore of the ocean. His companions—

[They] said: "For those who descend upon the ocean, life and death are not known. Let us all undertake the *poṣadha* endowed with the eight limbs. They agreed, saying, "So be it," and the *poṣadha* was undertaken. They set out upon the ocean. And while they were in the midst of the ocean, their ship was destroyed, being struck by adverse winds and other calamities; because of that, everyone—
They had passed away. And Maitrāyajña, having taken his chief disciples and a bound copper vessel, crossed to the shore of the ocean.

While wandering about, he saw a city with golden walls, endowed with parks, groves, and lotus ponds; it was perfumed with incense, strewn with loose flowers, and hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands.
Then four apsarases emerged. They took him by the hand and led him into the city.

He sported with them for many years—for many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years. They said to him, "Noble son, this region of the earth is unknown to you; it was unknown to us."

"You must not go out. If you do go out, you must by no means proceed facing north. After some time, he went out from there. As he proceeded further, he saw a city with walls made of silver, endowed with groves and woods, and so on, as described before. From that city as well, eight *apsarases* emerged; by them also, he was...
Having been taken, he was led inside. He sported with them for many years;

he sported for many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years, as described before. Then, after some time, he emerged. Wandering further, he again saw a city, complete with parks and surrounded by a wall made of lapis lazuli.
It was endowed with groves, endowed with lotus ponds, perfumed with incense, strewn with loose flowers, and hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands.

From that place as well, sixteen *apsarases* emerged. Together with them, he sported for many years, as described previously. They said to him: "Noble son, this region of the earth is new to you. From this pleasure grove..."

"Therefore, you must not go out. And even if you do go out, you must by no means go facing north. After some time, he went out from there. Wandering further, he saw a city with crystal walls, likewise endowed with gardens, groves, and lotus ponds.

It was perfumed with incense, strewn with loose flowers, and hung with clusters of silk ribbons and garlands. From that place as well, thirty-two apsarases emerged. Together with them, he sported for many years, many hundreds of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years.
They said to him, "Noble son, this region of the earth is new to you. From this...

"One must not depart from the monastery; furthermore, if you do depart, one must not go facing north. Due to their negligence, he became weary of pleasure and departed. As he went facing north, he entered a thorn forest. Then he saw a city with a wall of black iron and entered it. As soon as he had entered—
And the city gate was closed. He looked upward; the wall grew higher and he heard a terrifying sound.
Standing there, he wondered, "What is this? He went toward it and then saw a man's wheel, bearing blades, cutting off his head. Terrified, he asked, "What is this, O man? It was a man from the hells.

He said, "This is a solitary hell. Maitrāyajña asked, "What evil deed did you commit? He replied, "In this Jambudvīpa, there was a city named Mahākośalī. There, I was the son of a great caravan leader. Once, I went to a park with five hundred companions. They said, 'Your father, the caravan leader, is our...'"
"There is a leader who, having gone to other lands, acquires wealth.
He visits the Land of Gold, Siṃhaladvīpa, and various other islands.
We too shall see foreign lands with you as our guide. Thus they promised, "We also will go."

I went home and asked my mother, "I wish to go to another country. My mother said to me, "Son, your father set out upon the ocean and went to another country, where he has already passed away. You are an only son;
there is abundant wealth remaining in the house. You must not go. I promised her that I would not go.

In this manner, he was turned back from falling at his feet for the second, third, and even the fourth time. After some time, I went to the park again and was told by my companions, "You must certainly go. I promised, "I shall go.
Then, as I was setting out, my mother stood at the gate, falling at my feet, and said, "Son, you ought not to abandon me."

Thus he spoke. I placed my foot upon his head and departed. Accompanied by five hundred companions, I went to the shore of the ocean. Having undertaken the *poṣadha* observance endowed with the eight limbs, I descended into the sea. As we set out for the Land of Gold, our ship was struck by adverse winds and other calamities and was destroyed. They all passed away; however, after many days, I alone—

Having somehow emerged from the ocean, I was then tormented by a city with golden walls—a place endowed with parks, endowed with groves, and endowed with lotus ponds; perfumed with incense, strewn with loose flowers, and hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands.
From that [city], four apsarases came forth, and by them I was led inside. ... until... (MKV 54)

Together with them as well, I sported for many years, many hundreds of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years. Then, after some time, as I was departing... [as before]. From there, the apsarases emerged. I was led inside by them, and so on, until: together with them as well, I sported for many years and many hundreds of years.

For many hundreds of thousands of years we played. In this same way, [we entered] the city made of beryl. From that too, sixteen *apsarases* emerged... from that too he emerged. I see a city made of crystal. As before, from that thirty-two *apsarases* emerged. Together with them as well, I played in the same manner... [I saw] the thorn forest.
I arrived. Eventually, I saw an iron city. I entered it. Once I had entered, the gate was closed behind me.
And here, as before... I see a sword-bearing wheel revolving above my head.
While I was standing there, the sword-bearing wheel descended upon my head. This happened because I turned away from my mother... [and so forth].

He had observed the poṣadha endowed with its eight limbs. As the ripening of that karma, he was born in each of the heavens in the four great cities; yet, having placed his foot upon his mother’s head, he departed. As the ripening of that karma, the sword-bearing wheel cuts off my head. Maitrāyajña reflected: "I too have performed this very same karma. It has now come upon me."

"This too is the ripening of my karma," said the man from hell. "Where are you from? Maitrāyajña replied, "In Jambudvīpa there is a great city named Tāmalipta; I am from there. I too must perform all of this.
The man from hell said, "Today I heard a voice in the sky: 'The ripening of your karma is exhausted.'"

"The son of a caravan leader named Maitrāyajña will arrive today after having performed this very deed. Maitrāyajña asked, "What is the food? He replied, "It is the pus and blood that flows from this very head as it is being cut off.
Having said this, the man passed away and fell down. Maitrāyajña became terrified and agitated in every way.
Having prostrated to his parents, he said: "Above,
spreading to the peak of existence, below to the Avīci hell,
and across in all directions to world-systems beyond counting— "

Having thought, "May all the sentient beings who have entered into the bodies of myself, gods, asuras, humans, nagas, and elemental spirits be happy," and having performed prostrations and a formal salutation to one's mother and father with one's whole being, one should make this aspiration:
And he made this vow: "Wherever I may be reborn, may I perform service for my mother and father.

Furthermore, for the sake of all those beings who are reborn in the individual hells (*pratyekanaraka*), I remain here. Homage to all those in the world, whether bound or liberated; may they protect me. Having said this, that man from the hell...
Remaining at that time, he made a vow once more and spoke again: "First,
for those beings who are bound by the fetters of death, rebirth, and bondage, from the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence— "
May they all, having passed their time in happiness, attain the Dharma-endowed Nirvana which is ageless and immutable.
Then that wheel, without touching his head, remained perpetually above him in the sky. And always...

It is said that his mother offered this blessing: "If there is for me any fruit of merit—whether from giving, or from moral conduct, or from celibacy, or from devotion to my husband—by that fruit of merit, may no evil befall my son wherever he may stay. And by that, it was well with him.

b) Just as in the *Śyāmajātaka*, when Prince Śyāma was struck by a poisoned arrow, the arrowhead was extracted and the poison destroyed by the benedictory words of his parents, whereby he who had died was restored to life; likewise, it was well for him. As it was said by the noble Śāradvatīputra in the *Dhanañjayasūtra* at Vajrarājagṛha: "His parents honored that brahmin equally."
When properly honored, they respond with compassion through a virtuous mind.
Indeed, this son, by virtue of his righteous actions and qualities, does not perform any evil deed.
This should be applied to the entire sutra, just as it was said by the Blessed One in the *Śivālaka-sūtra* regarding that householder’s son and his parents: [they say], "O householder’s son..."

Established in five states, he causes others to be established in those same five states. Furthermore, O householder’s son, for that person who has been shown compassion by his parents, growth is to be expected in this way:
dwelling there with joy as his sustenance, he passes away after a full sixty thousand years.

d) Just as King Ajātaśatru passed away while the full lifespan of a denizen of hell was not yet exhausted; because actions are never fruitless, he once suffered from an exceedingly severe headache. e) In this regard, the service rendered to his parents by Maitrāyaṇīputra, who had made a formal vow, should be recounted—just as in the Śyāma-jātaka, where his blind parents were cared for by him when he had become an elephant. In hundreds of other Jātakas, f) then the Blessed One, knowing the time had come, addressed the monks: "It might be, monks, that you think it was someone else..."
"One should not view it thus that at that time, on that occasion, he was the caravan leader’s son named Maitrāyajña.
Rather, it should be seen that I myself was, at that time, on that occasion, the caravan leader’s son named Maitrāyajña.
Therefore, monks, you who have faith in my words should be respectful toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."

"You must be respectful. You must be respectful toward your mother and father, and toward your teachers and preceptors. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves. For one who has thus gone to another land experiences pleasure and pain; just as Maitrāyaṇīputra, having gone to another land, experienced individual heaven and individual hell in that very same birth. (MKV 57)
And it has been experienced. When one who has gone to another region experiences pleasure or pain, this is karma with ripening in another region.

g) The Blessed One demonstrates this: "As it is toward me, so it is toward my parents; for those who act according to the instructions of teachers and preceptors, the ripening is equal both in this world and in the next. How is the ripening of karma equal in this world? As follows:
In Śrāvastī, a poor man, upon seeing the Blessed One eating together with the community of disciples, felt faith in his heart.
By that act, he accumulated a great store of merit and performed a deed conducive to sovereignty. That very act was also the seed of liberation.
Knowing this, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
Those who there rejoice, and those who perform services for them—their reward shall not be deficient; they too are partakers of that merit.
This very point is the origin of the verse.
Mental states are preceded by the mind, have the mind as their chief, and are swift as the mind.
If one speaks or acts with a pure mind, happiness follows them like a shadow that never departs.

Having passed away from there, he was reborn among the gods. Just as in the case of the Pratyekabuddha named Tagaraśikhī: during a famine, a poor man offered him some soup, and on that very day he was consecrated as king in that city; subsequently, after some time, he became a Pratyekabuddha, as this Pratyekabuddha is recited in another Sūtra. (MKV 58)
Named Tagaraśikhin. Such, then, is the ripening of the fruit of a visible mental clarity toward the Blessed One.

How is it with respect to one's mother and father? It is as in the case of Maitrāyajña, the son of the caravan leader, who, having returned from four expeditions at his mother’s word, experienced the happiness of each of the heavens in four great cities. That, however, was for him—

It is the seed of liberation. Likewise, there is a visible ripening of the fruit even toward one’s mother and father. i) How is it that by harboring malice toward the Blessed One or toward one’s mother and father, one goes to hell? It is said: Devadatta, having harbored malice toward the Blessed One, fell into the great Avīci hell. Similarly, in the region of Sindhu, [at] Rauruka...

There was a city named Śikhaṇḍinagara. There, the prince Śikhaṇḍin, having caused his father to be killed, fell into hell. Thus, by corrupting one's mind toward the Blessed One or toward one’s mother and father, rebirth in hell occurs.

For that reason, is there no difference [between these cases]? It is said: there is a great difference. The Blessed One has accumulated a vast store of merit produced from roots of goodness acquired over many hundreds of thousands of kalpas.

The Buddha is the producer of the path that has not yet arisen; he teaches the path for the sake of awakening. Faith placed in him yields immeasurable fruit and ripening, culminating ultimately in nirvāṇa. Yet, the path to liberation is unknown to one's mother and father. Furthermore, not every word of one's parents should be carried out; there are some whose minds are afflicted by false views who speak to their children [in such a way].

"Come, lead me to my destruction; that will be for your benefit and for my happiness. Or: "Throw me over a precipice or cast me into fire. That must certainly not be done. For what reason? Because having caused the death of one's mother and father, one will inevitably go to hell. For this very reason, it was forbidden by the Blessed One.
One who has killed his mother or father should not be ordained; for him there is no going forth, no full ordination, and no attainment of the fruits [of the path].
Having excluded such a person, others are equal and identical to their mothers and fathers, as well as to their teachers and preceptors. And in what way are they equal?
Has it not been said by the Blessed One: "The affection of parents for their child persists even to the very marrow of the bones"?

In this way, there is no going forth for one who has not been permitted by his mother and father. Just as the noble Rāṣṭrapāla, Śoṇa, and others were not ordained by the Blessed One without having first obtained permission from their parents, even today they do not ordain those who have not been permitted.
And just as when the Blessed One had gone forth, Śuddhodana’s eyes vanished due to grief for his son. It is said:
Parents desire a son, hoping for five things: "When he has grown up, he will support us once we have become old;
he will perform our duties; he will become the master of our wealth; he will offer the ancestral funeral cakes when we have passed away;
and the lineage of our family will endure for a long time. Hoping for these five things, they desire a son.

Parents desire a son; teachers and preceptors do not act in this way. Rather, placing compassion alone at the forefront, they think: "How might he bring an end to this wheel of saṃsāra that has been turning since time immemorial? As stated by the Blessed One in the Vinaya: "The teacher regards his disciple as a son, and the disciple likewise regards the teacher as a father."

It happens thus. In this way, they will be happy, mutually dependent upon one another. Thus, preceptors and instructors are exactly equal to parents. As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Cakravarti-sūtra*: "By the ripening of what karma does a wheel-turning monarch [obtain] the elephant-treasures and the horse-treasures?"

And he obtains them. For a long time, as a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), he has personally carried his mother or father on his shoulders, or caused them to be conveyed by means of chariots and the like. He has personally carried his teachers (ācārya) and preceptors (upādhyāya), or caused them to be conveyed.
As the maturation (vipāka) of that karma, the wheel-turning monarch obtains the treasures of elephants and horses. For this reason also...

Parents and teachers—both preceptors (*ācārya*) and instructors (*upādhyāya*)—are equal. Nevertheless, there is another distinction: for householders, parents are to be honored; for those who have gone forth (*pravrajita*), it is the preceptors and instructors alone who are to be honored. This is as the Mahīśāsakas of a different lineage maintain regarding the origin of the matter in the Vinaya, just as the Blessed One said: "O monks, [do not [disrespect] preceptors and instructors...]"

"One should travel to another region without having asked for permission. Why? Monks, there may be an obstacle to life, an obstacle to the holy life, or an obstacle to the bowl and robes. Once upon a time, monks, there was a son of a caravan leader named Maitrāyajña. This avadāna should be recited exactly as it stands. In this very same way, the teachers and preceptors are equal.

And [the same applies] to one's mother and father. As it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, even if one were to carry one's mother and father on one's shoulders and wander throughout Jambudvīpa, providing them with all necessary support, and were to give gold and bullion throughout the four continents—even so, no recompense would have been made for one's mother and father."

Furthermore, whoever inspires faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and establishes them in the five precepts—the virtues beloved by the Noble Ones—it is in this way that children repay their parents. And all of this, the teachers and preceptors perform for them. As the Blessed One said in the *Dakṣiṇāvibhaṅga-sūtra*: "Just as, Ānanda, a person..."

Relying upon that person, one goes for refuge to the Buddha, goes for refuge to the Dharma, and goes for refuge to the Saṅgha; and the training precepts as they have been taught should be recited. Ānanda, it is impossible for that person to repay that other person even by means of merely saluting and rising from one's seat; for even teachers and preceptors are far more distinguished than one’s mother and father.
Just as Mahākātyāyana inspired faith in the western regions beginning with Avanti; and just as the noble Madhyandina, having disciplined five hundred *nāgas* in Kaśmīra, inspired faith in that land,
and having brought saffron from Lake Anavatapta, established it in Kaśmīra— which even today is enjoyed by the world.

A monastery was built, and even today they continue to reside right there. Just as the noble Gavāmpati inspired faith in a hundred-yojana region on the Golden Land, and just as Pūrvavideha was inspired with faith and monasteries were built by the noble Piṇḍolabhāradvāja, [they remain] even today in that very place.

They dwell there. Just as by the noble Mahendra the rākṣasas, beginning with Vibhīṣaṇa, were established in the precepts on Siṃhaladvīpa and the land was converted; and just as in the *Adhyardhaśataka-sūtra* it is said that by the noble Pūrṇa, five hundred lay followers (*upāsaka*) [were established] in the city of Śūrpāraka. (MKV 64)

They were inspired with faith, and the Candanamāla monastery was constructed. Just as the Blessed One traveled there through the air together with five hundred bhikṣus and inspired the multitude of people with faith—what is the use of mentioning the name of each individual bhikṣu, since the Blessed One has already attained parinirvāṇa? Whosoever among the bhikṣus was disciplined...

Whether they be bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, all of them have been disciplined by the bhikṣus alone. And whoever has been inspired with faith by someone, that person is their teacher (ācārya) and preceptor (upādhyāya). ... These [bhikṣus] are the Blessed One’s mothers and fathers; desiring their sons, they look toward five benefits. But the teachers and preceptors, out of compassion, teach the Dharma of Nirvāṇa. By this also...

For this reason, teachers and preceptors are far more distinguished than one's mother and father. Therefore, the Blessed One said thus: "O monks, those who have faith in my words should cultivate supreme confidence in the Blessed One;
they should cultivate supreme confidence in the Dharma, in the Saṅgha, in their mother and father, and in their teachers and preceptors. That will be for your benefit."
"For the benefit and happiness for a long night. This is an action whose maturation occurs in another place.
XXXIII. What is the action endowed with which a person, having first been happy, later becomes unhappy?
It is said: In this case, a certain person, when asked for a gift, first joyfully promises it, being delighted.

He gives. Having given, he indeed becomes remorseful. When he is reborn among humans, he is born into families that are wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments; yet later, those enjoyments of his go to ruin and exhaustion, and he subsequently becomes poor, just like the noble Gopaka. It is said that this occurred because [he had acted thus] toward the Perfectly Awakened One Kakutsunda.
A cow was given to the community of monks. Later, he was censured by others, who said, "This was not given well.
Because of that, his mind became corrupted. Wherever he was reborn, there he became very wealthy;
later, due to that corruption of mind, he became poor. Even in his final existence, in the city of Rājagṛha...

He was reborn in a certain house. As he was being born, his mother passed away. Because he had killed his mother and because he was born under the *mūla* constellation, [his father thought], "This child will root out our family; he is inauspicious. Thinking thus, he was abandoned by his mother in the cemetery along with her. Even there, milk flowed from one of the mother's breasts for him, solely through the power of his merit.

When he had grown up, the Blessed One went there and ordained him. The Blessed One related all of this in due order to the monks: "In this way, having first given a milk-cow out of a state of faith, he later became remorseful;
this is the fruit of that karma. However, that former clarity of mind was itself his seed of liberation. Just so...

In the great city of Campā, there was a householder’s son named Īśvara. He sent all his wealth into the hands of his servants to engage in trade in the four directions. All of that, having gone to foreign lands, was lost. He himself became a laborer for others. This is the karma endowed with which a person, having previously been happy, later becomes miserable.
XXXIV. What is the action endowed with which a person, having first been miserable, later becomes happy?

It is said: In this case, a certain person, having undertaken the practice of giving, promises when asked; he gives with difficulty, but having given the gift, he subsequently experiences joy. When he is reborn among humans, he is born among the poor.
He is born into noble families. Subsequently, his enjoyments increase. In this regard, the *avadāna* of Aniruddha should be told.
It is said that in Rājagṛha, he gave an alms-offering of śyāmāka rice to a Pratyekabuddha who was staying above him. On that very day...

Thus, the king, being pleased, granted him eight great villages; yet that was his final poverty. As it is stated in the *Pūrvāparāntaka-sūtra* regarding his very prediction: and as it is told how, in Śrāvastī, a poor man, having begged for seeds from his own kinsmen, took them to a field for the purpose of plowing. His wife, having placed a vessel at another's house, [took] rice...

The meal was prepared and brought. Then the Blessed One said to Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, and the others: "Alms should first be accepted at the house of such-and-such a householder. They all went there one after another, and alms were obtained by them all. Thereafter, the Blessed One [proceeded].

He had already departed. That woman, having conceived faith, gave all the remaining food to the Blessed One and made this aspiration: "O Blessed One, by this root of merit, may I never again fall into poverty. "So be it," the Blessed One replied. On that very day, a great treasure appeared for her. Having heard this—

King Prasenajit went to that house. He said, "Our former kings deposited these dinars there. The householder took them from him and gave a handful full to him; they turned into charcoal. The king gave more to the householder; they turned into gold. Then King Prasenajit was filled with wonder and went to the Blessed One.
He reported this. The Blessed One said: "Householder, that which is produced from merit is not to be accepted. And all of that was related in due order.

Thus, when such a donor is asked with difficulty, he agrees; he gives with difficulty, and having given, he gladdens his mind. For that reason, having previously been poor, he later becomes very wealthy.

It occurs as follows. This is the action endowed with which a person, having first been miserable, later becomes happy. XXXV. What is the action endowed with which a person is happy both before and after?
It is said: In this case, a certain person, when asked for a gift, promises it with joy and gives it with joy; even after having given it...

And he becomes full of joy. When he is reborn among humans, he is reborn into wealthy families, possessing great riches and great enjoyments. Herein, the maturation of the four patrons, beginning with Miṇḍhaka, in the city of Bhadrika must be told. It is said that by them the Pratyekabuddha Tagaraśikhī was provided with almsfood. Herein is the Vinaya-avadāna.
It should be stated: this is the action endowed with which a person is happy both before and after. XXXVI. What is the action endowed with which a person is miserable both before and after?
It is said: here, a certain person is deprived of a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). He does not give gifts, nor by that...

Some evil karma has been committed. When he is reborn among humans, he is reborn into poor families where food and drink are meager, as described in the avadāna of the poor boy in Śrāvastī. It is said that once, while the Blessed One was wandering for alms in Śrāvastī, there occurred what is known as the "Twelfth Day of the Sugarcane Festival" (ikṣudvādaśī) in Śrāvastī.
The Blessed One obtained some sugarcane. At a certain house-door stood a poor boy who asked the Blessed One for sugarcane. The Blessed One gave him one stalk. He asked for more.
The Blessed One said, "Child, speak; if you say 'I do not want it,' I will give you more. He replied:

“Blessed One, I have never before said, ‘I do not wish [to give]. The Blessed One said, “Child, say instead: ‘Blessed One, I do not wish [to keep anything]; I shall give everything. Because of his greed for sugarcane, he had said, “I do not wish [to give]. The Blessed One gave him everything. Then the Venerable Ānanda asked, “Blessed One, what is this? The Blessed One said, “Ānanda, this man has never [before] [refused] forms, tastes, smells, touches, and so forth.”
He had never before been satiated, nor had he ever once said, "I do not desire it. Thus, this statement of his will serve as the reason for [the claim] that he does not desire it. And it is said:
"This utterance, 'I do not desire it,' has never been spoken by him."
"Whence come forms and sounds, and whence indeed smells and touches?"—thus constantly praying in this way, the fool wanders about;
yet with great joy he utters these words: "I do not desire them."
The cause is this very state of having few desires, which will belong to him.
This is the action endowed with which a person becomes miserable both before and after.
XXXVII. What is the action endowed with which a person becomes wealthy yet miserly? It is said: in this case, by one who [possesses] only a small amount...
A gift may have been given to one who is virtuous and a worthy recipient, yet the mind of renunciation has not been cultivated.

When such a person is reborn among humans, they are born into wealthy families with great riches and great enjoyments. Because of that specific act of giving, since the mind of renunciation was not further cultivated by them, through that karma they become miserly.

As in the *avadāna* of the householder Hilliśāla in Śrāvastī. It is said that in a previous birth he was miserly. Then, a pratyekabuddha named Tagaraśikhī arrived at his house door. When the alms were being given to him, he saw it being offered by [the householder].

He did not give alms to the monk Kṣavaṇaya, and having been ordained, he fell away from the religious life. Having experienced divine and human prosperities as a result of that karma, he was reborn in Śrāvastī as the son of a preeminent family; being stingy, he died. King Prasenajit took his property, which was childless, and it was recorded in the *Śatavarga-āgama* among the *Prasenajit-saṃyukta* sections as "the king's scattered wealth."

The Discourse on the Name. Prasenajit said to the Blessed One: "Lord, a man of the foremost family has passed away here. I have taken possession of his wealth, which was left without an heir. The Blessed One asked: "Great King, how much of this householder's property have you taken? He replied: "Lord, one hundred times one hundred thousand [gold pieces], and the remaining wealth is immeasurable."
[The King asked: "Why has he not been struck [by lightning]? The Blessed One said: "Great King, this is his seventh instance of receiving wealth without having a son.
