Because he once provided alms-food to the Pratyekabuddha named Tagaraśikhī, that specific karma of his has been exhausted; however, he has not cultivated any other root of merit. Therefore, tonight, during the first watch of the night, he is being cooked in the Mahāraurava hell."
Thereupon the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Wealth, grain, gold, cattle, horses, jewels, and earrings; slaves, laborers, servants, and all other dependents."
When one is dying, nothing follows [along], nor does anything go taking it with [the person].
Whatever has been done by him—whether virtuous or evil—that indeed becomes his own; and that he takes with him as he goes.
Therefore, accumulate a store of merit for the sake of the future life; for merits are remembered as the foundation for living beings in this world and the next.
O dear kinsmen, this body remains at home, while [the self] stays in the cemetery.
Both good deeds and evil deeds follow one who departs.
This person becomes wealthy yet is stingy.
XXXVIII. What is the karma endowed with which a person becomes poor yet is generous? It is said:

In this case, a certain person has given much charity to animals and to humans who are immoral and unchaste. Again and again, he has cultivated a mind of renunciation. When he is reborn among humans, he becomes poor yet generous due to that practice of giving. However, because he gave gifts to those who were unworthy recipients, he is poor.

As it is related in the Vinaya concerning Śrāvastī, there is an account of a weaver. He was generous yet poor; he had repeatedly cultivated a mind of renunciation. This is the karma endowed with which a person becomes poor yet generous.
XXXIX. What is the karma endowed with which a person becomes wealthy and generous? It is said: in this case, by a certain individual...

A person has given much in alms to those who are virtuous and worthy recipients. Furthermore, they have repeatedly cultivated the mind of renunciation. By virtue of that karma, when they are reborn among humans, they are born into wealthy families with great riches and great enjoyments. Moreover, because they have repeatedly cultivated the mind of renunciation, they become generous themselves.

It happens as follows: it is said that by Anāthapiṇḍada, the Jetavana was offered to the Perfectly Enlightened One Krakucchanda, and a monastery was built. Likewise for the Perfectly Enlightened Ones Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Sarvārthasiddha.
Furthermore, he will offer [the land] covered with gold to Maitreya. This is the deed endowed with which [he possesses this merit].

A person becomes wealthy and generous. XL. For which person is the lifespan exhausted, but not the karma? It is said: that person who, having passed away from hell, is reborn in hells; having passed away from the animal realm, is reborn among animals; having passed away from the world of Yama, is reborn in the world of Yama; or having passed away from the gods, is reborn among the gods.

Just as the Brahmin Varṣākāra, having died again and again, was reborn as a monkey; just as the previously mentioned householder in Kaśmīra was reborn again and again as an animal; and just as a certain poor householder in Śrāvastī died, and at his house door stood an ox with its shoulder wounded. He...

A householder whose mind was attached to his home was reborn as a worm on the shoulder of that very ox. As soon as he was reborn, he was eaten by a crow. Again, he was reborn as a worm in that same place. In this manner, having passed away, he died seven times in a single day and was eaten by a crow as soon as he was reborn. Just as it was with the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana in Magadha...

While wandering for alms, he arrived at the door of a certain house. In that house, the householder, together with his wife, was eating a meal consisting of various kinds of fish and meat. His son sat upon a couch, and a black bitch stood before him; she was tossing the fish bones to him. Then the householder [beheld] Mahāmaudgalyāyana.

Having seen him, he said, "Go, noble sir; there is no one here who will give alms. He then set out. Now, at that house-door, some learned men who had arrived from another region were already standing;

seeing him, they were struck with wonder, exclaiming, "Oh, what a marvel! This man is indeed the foremost among those possessed of supernatural powers (ṛddhimat), by whom the two Naga kings, Nanda and Upananda..."

Vinīta and Vaijayanta were present, and the palace was shaken by his left big toe; Śakra was struck with wonder, for he who could traverse the triple-thousandfold world system in the blink of an eye was dismissed without being given alms. Then the Elder, in order to stir their spiritual urgency, said: "Child, this is no marvel. The men asked: "Then what else is a marvel?"

"This is the cause of my amazement. He said: "This householder who is eating his meal with various kinds of fish meat—this fish was his father. Having repeatedly pulled out many fish from this pond behind his house, he ate them. Having passed away, he has been reborn right here as this very fish."
This very person is being devoured again and again after being repeatedly pulled out; and right here he is reborn over and over again.

This female dog is the mother of this very householder. Due to the fault of greed, she gave no gift whatsoever, nor did she practice ethical conduct; she merely guarded her wealth for the sake of her family lineage. Her mind remains attached to that very house.

Having died, she was reborn among dogs; having died again and again, she was reborn in this very place. And throughout the entire night, she wanders all around the house, thinking, "Lest someone enter here. Now, as for this son who has been placed upon the couch, he is the secret husband of this very woman, and this has been heard by the householder: "This is your wife."
"She has become infatuated with another man. Thus, under the pretext of going to another village, this householder departed from his home;

meanwhile, this woman lay down with another man. This very night, the householder returned and killed a man. His mind being attached to this same woman, through that very bond of affection, he was conceived in her womb. Behold!

"Child, he who was his father, his flesh he eats; she who was his mother, his progenitor, to her he gives the fish-bones and scales; and him who was his enemy, a paramour killed by him in anger, he supports upon his lap. Such is the fault of *saṃsāra*; one must cultivate world-weariness (*nirveda*). This is the cause for wonder here. Then that monk, Mahāmaudgalyāyana—
He has summarized this entire meaning in a verse for the sake of inspiring a sense of urgency in future generations, as it is said: "The world,
shrouded in the darkness of delusion, eats the flesh of its father, casts thorns at its mother, and nourishes the paramour of its wife."
This person is one whose lifespan (*āyus*) is exhausted, but not their karma.
XLI. For which person is the karma exhausted, but not the lifespan? It is said: he who, having previously been happy, later becomes unhappy;
or he who, having previously been unhappy, later becomes happy. For this person, the karma is exhausted, but not the lifespan.

XLII. For which person is both karma and lifespan exhausted? It is said: that person who, having passed away from hell, is reborn among animals; having passed away from the animal realm, is reborn in the world of Yama; having passed away from the world of Yama, is reborn among humans;
and having passed away from there, is reborn among the gods. As, for example, the merchant’s son in Śrāvastī who went to a garden for the sake of flowers.

Following his wife's words, he climbed an *aśoka* tree, but that branch broke; he fell upon a stone slab and passed away. A great crowd of people was weeping there. Then, some monks who had gone for their midday rest saw this and, filled with agitation, reported it to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, oh, how impermanent is this! Here in the garden, the young son of a householder—"

"Having finished his enjoyment, he fell from the *aśoka* tree and passed away. A great multitude of people gathered there, and a sound like the wailing of the Raurava hell was heard. The Blessed One said: 'Monks, this very son of a householder was previously reborn in a certain nāga family in the great ocean. There, as soon as he was born, while playing together with women, he was seized by a garuḍa.'"

He was devoured. There, the Naga maidens wept; here, women weep. And he, at the word of whichever woman he had climbed upon the Aśoka tree, brought destruction upon her. "It was through her fault that I climbed the tree. Enraged, he passed away and was reborn in the hells. For this person, karma is exhausted and his lifespan has ended.
XLIII. For which person are both merits and life-span exhausted?

It is said: as in the case of that very householder Hilliśālī. As the Blessed One said: "Furthermore, O Great King, for that householder, that wholesome karma was completely exhausted and no other was performed. He will [die] this very first night..."
He is cooked in the Raurava hell. Just as King Prasenajit, having fallen from his kingdom, arrived at Rājagṛha;

there, while he was throwing old radish leaves into his mouth and eating them, he was struck by a man. With his mouth full of dark [blood], he then died. He had previously been a Pratyekabuddha. [Of that former one...]

As a result of the ripening of alms-food: this person whose lifespan and merits have both been exhausted. XLIIIbis. For which person is neither lifespan nor karma exhausted, but rather the afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted? It is said:
for the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and the pratyekabuddha. This is that person whose...
It is not that life-span is exhausted, nor is karma; rather, it is the afflictions (*kleśa*) that are exhausted.

XLIV. What kind of person is happy in body but not in mind? It is said: an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has performed meritorious deeds is happy in body but not in mind—such as wealthy brahmins and householders, and King Māndhātṛ. This is that person.
Happy in body but not in mind.

XLV. What kind of person is happy in mind but not in body? It is said: for example, an Arhat who is devoid of merit is happy in mind but not in body; as was the case with the noble Śroṇottara, it is said, because in a previous birth he [had seen] a Pratyekabuddha bathing.

A ball of cow dung mixed with *kapikacchu* was given for the purpose of bathing. By the ripening of that karma, his body is being shattered by leprosy. Thus it is said in verse: "Karmas are surely more powerful than even those karmas that are like thunderbolts."
In this state, having come under its control, I experience sufferings and karmic results.

It is like the case of Jaṅghākāśyapa. He had indeed promised a Pratyekabuddha in Vārāṇasī, "I shall give you food. After much great exertion, when the time for it was nearly past, he finally gave him the food. He...

Due to that karma, even though he has become free from passion in his final birth, he wanders for alms in the forenoon; when the time [for the meal] is nearly past, he somehow obtains food. Thus his name is Jaṅghākāśyapa. This person is happy in mind, but not in body.

XLVI. What kind of person is one who is happy in body and mind? It is said: it is the Arhat whose outflows are exhausted and who has accomplished merit, such as Bakula, the son of King Dharmayaśas of Kaśmīra. For his was the lion’s roar: "Venerable sirs, for eighty years since I went forth, never before have I experienced even a single illness, not even so much as a mere headache."

It is said that in Vārāṇasī, having been a merchant of perfumes, he invited the Perfectly Awakened One Kakutsunda, together with his community of disciples, to provide medicinal treatment for the sick; however, a single myrobalan fruit was taken by a monk who was an Arhat. As a result of that karma, he became free from ailment. The Blessed One has stated that health is the supreme gain, as the noble Aniruddha relates.
Venerable ones, as the ripening of that very alms-food, he was reborn seven times among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa host,

and seven times he exercised sovereignty among humans. And through the ripening of that same alms-food, he became an attainer of the fruit of arhatship, [receiving] the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.

He is a recipient [of gain]. For instance, during a famine, five hundred monks were given to him by the Blessed One. Through the power of his merit, divine and inexhaustible food appears for them all. This person is happy in body and happy in mind. XLVII. What kind of person is neither happy in body nor happy in mind? It is ordinary persons who have not performed meritorious deeds and whose family lineage has been destroyed.

Deprived of clothing, food, and drink, they indeed wander about in the houses of others. Likewise, they are afflicted by diseases such as leprosy, consumption, cough, fever, anemia, ringworm, and insanity;
they are maimed in their hands and feet and deprived of sight. This person is happy neither in body nor in mind.
XLVIII. What is the karma endowed with which a person, though born in the miserable states (apāya), becomes handsome and pleasing?

One with a smooth body, smooth skin, and pleasing eyes is beautiful to behold. It is said: there is a person who, being possessed of immorality arising from passion, is reborn in the miserable states—such as peacocks, parrots, mainas, ducks, ruddy geese, and so forth.
This is the karma by which a person, though reborn in the miserable states, becomes handsome, attractive, and possesses a smooth body.
One with smooth skin, pleasing to the eyes, and beautiful to behold.

XLIX. In this regard, what is the karma endowed with which a person, having been reborn in the states of woe, becomes ill-colored, coarse-bodied, and terrible to behold? It is said: it is that person who is possessed of immorality arising from hatred.

One is reborn in the states of woe—such as among lions, tigers, crows, jackals, black snakes, pretas, piśācas, and so forth. This is the karma by which one, having been reborn in the states of woe, becomes ill-colored, with a coarse body and a terrifying appearance.
In that regard, what is the karma endowed with which a person, having been reborn in the states of woe, becomes foul-smelling?

One with dull faculties is one whose faculties are unmanifested. It is said: that person who, being possessed of immorality arising from delusion, is reborn in the states of woe—such as the muskrat, worms, pythons, lice, flies, and so forth, or like the twenty species of worms within the body. This is the karma endowed with which a person, having been reborn in the states of woe, is foul-smelling.
One becomes crooked in one's faculties and indistinct in one's faculties.

LI. There are ten unwholesome paths of action (*daśākuśalāḥ karmapathāḥ*). Which are the ten? Threefold bodily action, fourfold vocal action, and threefold mental action. Through the maturation (*vipāka*) of these ten unwholesome paths of action, [the following] ten external...

There is an increase of [unwholesome] states. LII. As the ripening (*vipāka*) of the unwholesome path of action that is the taking of life, the vitality and splendor of the earth disappear; and by the ripening of that very same action, one becomes short-lived. LIII. As the ripening of the unwholesome path of action that is taking what is not given, thunderbolts, parrots, locusts, mice, insects, and so forth—those which devour the crops—arise upon the earth. By the ripening of that very same action...
Through the ripening [of that karma], one encounters the ruin of wealth.

LIV. Through the ripening of the unwholesome path of action that is sexual misconduct, foul-smelling grasses, darbha-grass, and so forth appear upon the earth. Through the ripening of that very same karma, they enter into well-furnished dwellings. Regarding this, there is a legend (avadāna).
The story of the previous birth of Kālodayin—during the descent of the gods—when he was the daughter of Śvabhrapada and the wife of the King of Kāśi, must be told.

As the ripening of the unwholesome path of action that is false speech, diseases of the mouth, teeth, and throat, as well as foul breath and so forth, arise (MKV 79). Through the ripening of that very same karma, one comes to experience the speaking of what is untrue.

LVI. As the maturation (*vipāka*) of the unwholesome path of action consisting of malicious speech (*piśunavacana*), gravel, potsherds, and other such things that involve painful contact appear upon the earth. Through the maturation of that very same karma, one suffers the misfortune of birth and the misfortune of friends;
furthermore, one's retinue becomes divided.

LVII. As the maturation (*vipāka*) of the unwholesome path of action consisting of harsh speech, there arise dust, dirt, wind, rain, and so forth. By the maturation of that very same karma, there occurs the hearing and seeing of unpleasant sounds. LVIII. As the maturation of the unwholesome path of action consisting of frivolous chatter (*saṃbhinna-pralāpa*), ravines, chasms, and so forth appear. By the maturation of that very same karma, their words become unacceptable.

LIX. As the maturation (*vipāka*) of the unwholesome path of action that is covetousness (*abhidhyā*), husks, straw, and the like appear among the crops such as rice, barley, and wheat. By the maturation of that very same karma, the enjoyments (*bhoga*) sought from others [are lost]. LX. As the maturation of the unwholesome path of action that is malice (*vyāpāda*), the crop becomes fruitless despite being sown in abundance. By the maturation of that very same karma, one becomes one to whom things appear disagreeable (*pratikūla-darśana*). LXI. As the maturation of the unwholesome path of action that is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), there are bitter and pungent states.

Furthermore, fruits such as the *picumanda*, *koṣātakī*, poisonous bitter gourds (*viṣatiktālābu*), and so forth, come into existence. As the ripening (*vipāka*) of the unwholesome path of action (*akuśalakarmapatha*) of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), one becomes a proponent of nihilism (*nāstikyavādin*). One holds the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) and finds faith in treatises such as those of the Lokāyata. This was the case with Prince Padāśva, who [was taught] by Kumārakāśyapa at Śvetikā.

The Lokāyatika has been refuted. Just as sentient beings cultivate these ten unwholesome paths of action, so too does there arise an excessive manifestation of these ten external things. And for this very reason, in the future time during the great eon of destruction (*mahāsaṃvartakalpa*), there will come a time when sesame seeds will exist, sesame paste will exist, and oil will exist.

There will be no sugarcane; there will be no sugarcane juice; there will be no molasses. There will be no candied sugar, nor will there be granulated sugar. There will be cows, there will be milk, and there will be curds, but there will be no fresh butter, no clarified butter, and no scum of clarified butter. In this manner, everything will gradually [disappear].
All flavors will disappear.

(MKV 81) LXII. What are the ten benefits of performing the act of joining the palms and prostrating before the Tathāgata’s shrines, such as the four great caityas and the Great Bodhi tree in Lumbinī in the Middle Country?
It is said: one obtains birth in the Middle Country; one obtains noble garments; one obtains a noble family;
one obtains a noble age; one obtains a noble voice; one obtains noble eloquence; one obtains noble faith; one obtains noble ethical discipline; and one obtains noble learning.
He attains it. He attains noble generosity; he attains noble mindfulness; he attains noble wisdom.
Here is its summary verse (*uddāna*): Regarding country, clothing, family, form, voice, eloquence, faith, morality, learning, and renunciation—one becomes mindful and possessed of wisdom.
Having thus produced serene confidence in the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the steadfast one gains the *añjali* [of respect].

[He attains] the noble destruction of the outflows along with wisdom. And it is said in the Sūtra: "Ānanda, whoever, while practicing the pilgrimage to the shrines, shall pass away with a serene mind, they will, upon the dissolution of the body, be reborn in the heavenly realms, just as an arrow shot [into the earth] remains fixed therein."

LXIII. What are the ten benefits of venerating a *caitya* of the Tathāgata? It is said: one becomes handsome; one possesses a beautiful voice; one’s speech is authoritative; having approached an assembly, one wins over the assembly; one becomes dear to gods and humans; one becomes influential; one comes into association with beings who are influential; [and one comes into association] with Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas.
And one meets [with favorable circumstances]. One becomes possessed of great wealth. One is reborn in the heavenly realms. And one quickly attains final nirvāṇa.
These are the ten benefits of venerating a stūpa of the Tathāgata.
LXIV. What are the ten benefits of giving an umbrella? It is said: One becomes like an umbrella for the world.

He becomes untormented in body and untormented in mind. Furthermore, he has performed and accumulated karma conducive to sovereignty; he repeatedly becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin), possesses great majesty, encounters beings of great majesty, and encounters Buddhas and the disciples of Buddhas.
He becomes one of great wealth; he is reborn in the heavenly realms; and he swiftly attains parinirvāṇa.

Here, the ripening of the fruit of the parasol offered at the stūpa of the Pratyekabuddha Bhagavat during the crossing of the Gaṅgā is described, as well as the account given by the noble Sundarananda regarding the bath of Jentāka and the anointing of the palm tree.
"And from the gift of a single parasol, I have attained this golden complexion.
In this manner, the maturation (*vipāka*) of the gift of a parasol should be described. And it is said:
(MKV 86) [notes only]
That which is borne is a preeminent staff of noble form,
its base-case adorned with a bow and a cord,
and a vast, stainless parasol resembling the orb of the moon.
Born from the gift of an umbrella by Jagaddhara,
this golden parasol, resplendent with its cloth and possessing a handle of jewels and gold, has become the very emblem of his glory.
That which is borne upon the head of the lord of men by the gift of a parasol— these are the ten benefits of giving a parasol to the Sustainer of the World.

LXV. What are the ten benefits of the gift of a bell? It is said: one becomes handsome; one becomes sweet-voiced; one becomes pleasant of speech; one speaks with the voice of a kalaviṅka bird; one’s words become authoritative; one is always full of joy; one repeatedly hears sounds of bliss; one is reborn in the heavens; and one possesses great wealth.

And one quickly attains final nirvāṇa. For example, Viśākhā, the mother of Mṛgāra, asked the Blessed One: "How may the fivefold musical ensemble always sound at my palace at all times? The Blessed One said: "Hang up a bell endowed with every musical tone. In this way, the sound of the fivefold musical ensemble will be present in your palace at all times, and it will be irreproachable. These are the ten virtues of giving a bell."

LXVI. What are the ten virtues of giving clothing? It is said: one has smooth skin; one has glossy skin; dust and dirt do not adhere to the body; one is endowed with a sense of shame and modesty; one is pleasant to behold; one possesses abundant clothing; and one obtains fine garments and bedspreads.

One becomes possessed of great enjoyments; one is reborn in the heavens and swiftly attains parinirvāṇa. As stated by the Blessed One in the *Devatāsūtra*: "One who gives clothing becomes endowed with a beautiful complexion. These are the ten qualities and benefits of giving clothing.
LXVII. What are the ten benefits of giving a seat? It is said: One becomes like a teacher to the world.

He becomes pleasant to behold; he becomes inspiring; he becomes approachable by wise people; his fame and renown become celebrated throughout the world; he abounds in happiness and mental well-being; he finds delight in his own country; there is no lack of seats for him; there is no lack of attendants; he possesses great wealth; and he is reborn in the heavenly realms.

And one quickly attains parinirvāṇa. These are the ten virtues of giving a seat. LXVIII. What are the ten benefits of giving a vessel? It is said: one becomes a fit vessel for virtues; one’s mental continuum becomes supple; one does not suffer from excessive thirst; and for one afflicted by thirst, water appears.
Nor is one reborn among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). One’s vessels become complete; one possesses great wealth; one is reborn in the heavens;
and one quickly attains final nirvāṇa (*parinirvāti*). These are the ten benefits of giving vessels.
LXIX. What are the ten benefits of giving food? It is said: one becomes strong; one becomes endowed with a beautiful complexion (*varṇavān*).
He becomes happy; he becomes eloquent; he becomes long-lived; he becomes approachable by great crowds;
he becomes pleasant to behold; he possesses great wealth; he is reborn in the heavenly realms; and he quickly attains parinirvāṇa.
As was said by the Blessed One to Prince Siṃha at Vaiśālī: "O Siṃha, by giving, one becomes beloved."
Virtuous people associate with them; they acquire a reputation for excellence; they enter the assembly with confidence; having passed away, they are reborn among the gods. And this verse was spoken:
"There, they rejoice, delight, and find joy."
Having surrendered themselves to the five strands of sensual pleasure and having carried out the word of the immeasurable Protector,
those disciples of the most excellent Sugata rejoice.
This fruit of giving was spoken by the Blessed One:
one is reborn in the heavens and swiftly attains parinirvāṇa. And it is said:
[food] well-prepared with various flavors and condiments...
He who, having considered the vessel and reflected upon the virtues of the noble Saṅgha, always gives at the proper time a gift that is pure and endowed with excellent fragrance and flavor.
Having attained long life, complexion, fame, strength, enjoyments, eloquence, and happiness both in heaven and here on earth, he is renowned for his supreme glory.
One goes from happiness to happiness and attains liberation at the end.
These are the ten virtues of giving food.
LXX. What are the ten virtues of giving vehicles? It is said: one comes to have delicate feet; one comes to have well-planted feet.
There is no exhaustion from the journey. One does not have many enemies. Again and again, one attains the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
There is no lack of vehicles such as elephants, horses, and so forth. One possesses great wealth and is reborn in the heavens.
And one quickly attains final nirvāṇa (*parinirvāti*).

a) As it is said in the *Devatāsūtra*: "The giver of a vehicle becomes happy; so too does he who gives sandals. And as it is said in the *Abhidharma-cakravartisūtra*: "By the ripening of what karma does a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) obtain mounts such as elephants and horses? For a long time, the universal monarch [has served] his mother, father, or preceptor..."

Or he carries [the load] on his shoulder, or causes it to be carried; or he carries [others] by means of elephants, horses, and so forth, or by means of palanquins and carriages; or he constructs difficult passages, or builds bridges; or he gives gifts of sandals; or out of compassion, he leads a caravan across a great wilderness. Through the ripening of that karma, a universal monarch (cakravartin) obtains elephants, horses, and so forth.
Mounted upon that, he traverses the earth bounded by the oceans in a fourth part of a day. These are the ten qualities of the gift of a vehicle.
(MKV 95) [Notes only] LXXI. What are the ten qualities of the gift of a shelter? It is said: One becomes a regional king; one becomes a king...
One becomes a regional ruler; one becomes a king, a sovereign of Jambudvīpa; one becomes a king, a sovereign of two continents;

one becomes a king, a sovereign of three continents; one becomes a king, a universal monarch (cakravartin) sovereign of the four continents. One possesses great wealth and is reborn in the heavenly realms, and swiftly attains final nirvāṇa.
As in the verse of the bhikṣuṇī Sumedhā:
"When the Blessed One Koṇāgamana was in the monastery, three friends among our household previously gave him that vihāra."

These verses belong to Sumedhā. There were also the bhikṣuṇīs Dharmadinnā and Viśākhā, the mother of Mṛgāra. Formerly, when they were poor women, they drove four stakes into the ground, placed a wooden frame over them, and invited the Buddha Konāgamuni. He rested there for a moment together with the bhikṣus. By those women, their minds...

They were rendered gracious. By that karma, he was reborn among the gods a hundred thousand times. He experienced immeasurable kingdoms as a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). In this regard, all the verses of Sumedha should be understood individually in detail. These are the ten virtues of providing shelter.

LXXII. What are the ten virtues of giving a drink? It is said: one becomes endowed with all the sense faculties; one has a serene face; one has a pure forehead; one has smooth skin; one becomes a speaker of coherent speech; one does not suffer from excessive thirst; for one who is thirsty, water appears; one is not reborn among the hungry ghosts (*preta*); one possesses great wealth; one is reborn in the heavens; and one quickly attains final nirvana (*parinirvāti*). As it has been said:
It possesses pleasing color, endowed with flavor and fragrance, increasing the delight of all the sense faculties,
timeless, and praised by virtuous persons.
But he who gives a beverage to the Saṅgha,
being once freed from thirst and free from sorrow,
experiences the four supreme tastes.
And having satisfied the world with the essence of the True Dharma, one reaches the exhaustion of thirst through happiness by means of happiness.
These are the ten virtues of the gift of a beverage.

LXXIII. What are the ten virtues of offering a garland? It is said: one becomes like a garland to the world; bodily foul odors depart and a fragrant scent appears; one is constantly fragrant and constantly adorned; one possesses an inseparable retinue; one is beloved by all people; one possesses great wealth; and one is reborn in the heavenly realms.
And he quickly attains parinirvāṇa.
And I [offer] a garland that is variegated, excellent, and fragrant.
One who, with a serene mind, offers [an object] into the reliquary containing the relics of the Sage, which brings joy and causes delight to men, indeed bestows [merit] upon the Tathāgatas.
With his limbs radiant with divine garlands and ornaments, having attained glorious happiness both here and in heaven,
he has his self adorned by the wreath of the factors of enlightenment.
One whose fragrance is the foremost of virtues attains supreme liberation.

Likewise, there was the daughter of a certain poor householder. Standing at the door, she saw the people of the countryside adorned with every ornament, enjoying themselves at a festival. She said to her father, "Adorn me as well. Her father replied, "From where would we have [the means]?"

It is an ornament for the poor. This region has performed meritorious deeds and has rendered service many times to the Blessed Buddha. Because of that karma, the *avadāna* of the elder Karṇeṣumana was told by him in detail. Thus, even a small amount of faith placed in the Blessed One becomes of great fruit. By her, her father was intensely entreated: "Give [it]!"

"I have this small dwelling here in front of me; I shall perform an offering to the Blessed One there. Afflicted by suffering and lacking any wealth, he made a garland out of straw and gave it. She took that straw garland, placed it upon the head of the Buddha image, prostrated at his feet, and said: "O Blessed One, by this root of merit..."

"May she not experience poverty again as she wanders through saṃsāra. On that very day, by virtue of her faith, she transcended her human female state and a divine form appeared. The king residing in that region appointed her as his chief queen. When she passed away, she was reborn among the gods. Furthermore, in her final existence, she was born in Campā into a family of the highest rank.

A daughter was born who was most excellent; a golden garland adorned with all kinds of jewels suddenly appeared upon her head. Her parents, filled with wonder, gave her the name Mālinī. And when the Blessed One, having attained full enlightenment, arrived at Campā from Rājagṛha, she approached him, and for her the Blessed One—

She gave the teaching on the Dharma, and having gone forth, she became an Arhatī. From the very moment that thought arose, [the garland] vanished from her with the thought, "May I no longer have a garland. Seeing this, a goddess who was struck with wonder recited a verse, as it is said:
"But having given a garland made of straw at the stūpa of the Sugata, that Mālinī..."
One obtains a garland of excellent gold and jewels, as well as the garland of the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*).
These are the ten qualities of giving a garland.
LXXIV. What are the ten qualities of giving loose flowers? It is said: one becomes like a flower for the world.
The sense-faculty of the nose is purified. The foul odor of the body departs, and a sweet fragrance appears.

The scent of his ethical discipline becomes renowned throughout the ten directions. He becomes worthy of approach and attains desirable qualities. He possesses great wealth and is reborn in the heavenly realms, where he swiftly attains final nirvāṇa.
a) Here, the ripening of the gift of each individual flower must be told regarding the faith that arose in Karṇeṣumana’s previous birth. As he himself said:
"By the gift of a single flower as an offering to a Buddha, for eighty koṭis of kalpas I did not experience an unfortunate rebirth; such is the fruit of that."
These are the ten virtues of offering loose flowers.

LXXV. What are the ten virtues of offering a lamp? It is said: one becomes a light for the world; the fleshly eye perishes; the divine eye appears; the darkness of ignorance is dispelled; and the light of knowledge arises.

One swiftly penetrates wholesome and unwholesome phenomena with wisdom. While wandering in *saṃsāra*, the darkness of ignorance does not arise. One possesses great wealth, is reborn in the heavens, and swiftly attains *parinirvāṇa*.
This is as stated in the *Abhidharma* in the analysis of the *Cakravarti-sūtra*: "By the ripening of what karma does one become a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*)?"

He obtains a precious jewel. For a long time, the universal monarch has offered lamps and single offerings of light; in the darkness, he has maintained jewel-lamps so that those who possess eyes may see forms, both level and uneven. And it is said:
And one obtains the eye praised by the Buddha—
that eye which is the supreme cause for the manifestation of forms here in this world.
By the gift of a lamp to the Sustainer of the World, one's splendor becomes superior; there is no need to look for further wealth,
for he who beholds auspicious deeds is exceedingly pleased.
Having attained happiness both in heaven and here on earth, one whose vision is purified attains tranquility.

In this regard, the account of the noble Aniruddha’s divine eye at Dīpa, as well as the account of the extraction of the eyes of the sages for the sake of their liberation, should be told. As follows:

By the offering of a garland of lamps, Dīpaṅkara attained Buddhahood. Furthermore, in Śrāvastī, one who was deprived of sight had a garland of lamps made; he became filled with faith and made a vow. As soon as he arose, his eyes were restored to their former state. These are the ten virtues of the gift of lamps.

LXXVI. What are the ten virtues of the gift of fragrance? It is said: one becomes like a fragrance for the world; the faculty of smell is purified; bodily foul odors depart; a sweet fragrance manifests; the fragrance of ethical discipline wafts through the ten directions; one becomes approachable; one obtains desirable qualities; and one possesses great wealth.
He is reborn in the heavenly realms and swiftly attains final nirvāṇa.

As it is stated in the *Abhidharma*, in the *Cakravarti-sūtra*: "By the ripening of what karma does a fragrance issue forth from the pores of the body of the female jewel (*strī-ratna*) of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), such as that of a casket of perfumes?"

For a long time, that woman offered fragrant ointments in the inner sanctums of caityas; she offered fragrant flowers and incense, and she performed the ritual bathing of stupas with perfumes. As the ripening of that karma, such a fragrance issues from the body of the Queen-Consort, the Jewel among Women, of the Universal Monarch, just like that of a casket of perfumes.
These are the ten virtues of offering incense. LXXVII.

What are the ten virtues of going forth (*pravrajyā*)? It is said: one has no craving for sons, wives, daughters, or wealth; one does not possess the grasping of sensual desire; one attains joy in dwelling in the forest; [one enters] the sphere of the Buddhas...

He cultivates [virtue]. He avoids the sphere of the foolish. He avoids those qualities that lead to an unhappy rebirth. He cultivates those qualities that lead to a happy rebirth. The gods envy him. He constantly obtains the going forth in the teaching of the Sugata.
These are the ten virtues of the going forth.

LXXVIII. What are the ten virtues of dwelling in the forest? It is said: one avoids social distraction; one cultivates seclusion; the mind becomes focused on the object of meditation; one does not fall into excessive busyness with worldly affairs; one attains mindfulness of the Buddhas; the body is never parted from joy, bliss, and mental well-being; and there are no obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

One attains meditative concentration with little effort. The words and phrases taught to one do not fade from memory. One understands in detail the meaning of the teachings exactly as they were heard. These are the ten virtues of dwelling in the forest. LXXIX. What are the ten virtues of being a mendicant who lives on alms? It is said: one’s walking meditation is perfected; one’s range of activity is well-mastered; and one’s pride is destroyed. (MKV 105)
He becomes one who joins himself with gain; he establishes others in merit; he illuminates the teaching of the Teacher;
he becomes a light for future generations; he does no harm to his fellow practitioners of the holy life;
he maintains a humble mind; and for a monk whose mind is intent on alms-food, all directions become favorable.
These ten qualities lead to [the practice of] living on alms-food (piṇḍapātika).

LXXX. The ten grounds of self-confidence (vaiśāradya). What are the ten? It is said: one enters a village with self-confidence; one departs from a village with self-confidence; one consumes alms-food with self-confidence; one teaches the Dharma in an assembly with self-confidence.
Confident, he enters the midst of the Saṃgha. Confident, he approaches his teachers and preceptors.

Confident and with a mind of loving-kindness, he instructs his disciples. Confident, he makes use of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. His words are authoritative and accepted. These are the ten grounds of self-confidence.
The Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra is completed.
